newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile minister slams U.S. magnate over park plans.
newsitem.headline: Chile minister slams U.S. magnate over park plans.

text.p: Chilean Defence Minister Edmundo Perez Yoma lashed out on Friday at an American millionaire in a spat over his plans to create a huge rainforest reserve in southern Chile.

Clothing tycoon Douglas Tompkins announced this week that he would delay plans to turn the forests into a national park until another government came to power due to "hostility" from the current administration.
"We find that his most recent attitudes are those of a foolish, arrogant person with attitudes which are irritating to us," Perez Yoma told reporters.

His outburst underlined the increasingly critical stance the government has taken against Tompkins who owns 280,000 acres (113,300 hectares) of virgin forests stretching from Chile's Pacific coast to the Andean border with Argentina.
Government officials and rightist politicians have accused Tompkins of trying to depopulate the frontier area with Argentina and pressurizing settlers to sell their land at knock-down prices.
"The country has tried for many years, rightly or not, to populate the extreme south...," Perez Yoma said.
"And it is not very pleasing, to say it politely, that someone comes and with the force of his money goes against a state policy which many Chilean governments have followed."
Tompkins' land is one of the last wilderness areas left in cool southern Chile and holds spectacular scenery including dramatic icy fjords and rare Andean larch forests.
Although environmentalists and leftists cheer the park project, President Eduardo Frei's government has become increasingly suspicious of the tycoon who founded the Esprit clothing empire.
"Now has arrived the moment for him to say what he is doing and what (aims) he is pursuing," Perez Yoma said.
In 1995, Frei prevented Tompkins from buying a property known as Huinay which separates the two large separate tracts of land he owns.
The magnate had planned to join the properties together to create a giant nature reserve which would eventually be open to the public.
Tompkins' plans have been blasted by nationalists who accuse him of trying to cut Chile in half.
His supporters charge critics of using nationalist rhetoric as a smokescreen for big timber and salmon-raising companies which want to buy up the land.
